title: How to add a voiceover to a screen recording without using your own voice
summary: Turn a rough screen recording into a narrated video with an AI voice: script cleanup, sync, product-name pronunciation, captions, and updates.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- You don't need to narrate a screen recording yourself. Talk through the workflow roughly while you record, turn that transcript into a clean script, and have an AI voice read it.
- The script decides the quality. The voice reads exactly what you give it, so every step should name the label on screen.
- Four things break once you're past the first video: narration drifting out of sync with the clicks, mispronounced product names, dead air during slow screens, and captions made from the wrong source.
- Pick one voice for the whole library. Many contributors with their own voices sound like many different videos.
- Generated narration pays off at the update. Changing a step means editing one line and regenerating that clip, not finding the person who recorded it.


You've recorded the workflow, and the audio is what's holding the video back. It was recorded on a laptop mic in an open office, it has three restarts in it, and there's an "um" every other sentence. Or the person who knows the workflow best would rather not narrate it at all.


An AI voiceover fixes both, as long as the script is clean and the narration stays in time with what's happening on screen. This guide walks through how to add one to a screen recording, the four problems that show up once you make more than a few videos, and how to keep the narration current when the product changes.


## What is an AI voiceover for a screen recording?


An AI voiceover for a screen recording is narration generated by a text-to-speech voice from a written script and laid over the recording in place of your own voice. The script usually starts as a transcript of rough narration spoken during the recording. It's cleaned up, voiced, and then synced to the clicks on screen.


The recording itself doesn't change. Viewers still see the real product, and only the audio is new.


## How do you add a voiceover to a screen recording without recording your voice?


The fastest route is to record first and write second. You talk through the workflow while you record, the rough audio becomes a transcript, and the transcript becomes the script the AI voice reads. Here are the steps, and what to check at each one.


1. **Record the workflow and talk through it as you go.** Use whatever microphone your laptop has, because nobody will hear this audio. It only exists to become the transcript, so say "select Reports, then Aging" rather than "click over here".
2. **Turn the transcript into a script.** Read every line against the screen it describes. Each instruction should be specific enough to follow without the video, and each label should match what's on screen exactly.
3. **Choose one voice and add your product names.** Use the same voice across your library, and add brand names and acronyms to a pronunciation dictionary before your first export, not after your fortieth.
4. **Generate the narration and check the sync.** Watch the full video once and look for any click that lands before or after the words describing it.
5. **Check the captions and export.** Make sure the captions come from the final narration, not the original script, and listen to the last five seconds of the export.


Clueso does the mechanical parts of steps two to five. Upload a recording, or[record your screen](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) in Clueso, and it transcribes your narration, removes the filler words, and rewrites the transcript into a script you can edit. It then reads the script back in the[AI voice](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) you choose and keeps it synced to what's on screen. Your job is to review the script, pick the voice, and check the result. AI voiceovers are on every plan, including Free, and the same recording also produces a[written step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) . For a single video, our[add a voiceover tool](https://www.clueso.io/tools/add-voiceover-to-video) walks through it in three steps.


## Should you write the script first or record first?


Record first in most cases. The alternative is to write the script, generate the narration, and then record your screen while clicking in time with the voice playing back. That turns the person recording into a performer, and it means writing every word before anyone has checked the screen, so every surprise during recording sends you back to the script.


Script-first still has its place. When a reviewer has to approve the exact wording before anything is produced, as with compliance content or anything legal reads, writing first gives them something to sign off.

## How do you keep an AI voiceover in sync with the screen?


Generated narration almost never matches the length of the screen action it describes. A tool has to close that gap somehow, usually by stretching or compressing the video to fit the audio. That's why some AI-narrated videos play slightly too fast, or land on a click a beat late.


The fix is to pin the moments that matter. A sync point ties a specific phrase in the script to a specific frame, so "select Export" plays as the cursor reaches the Export button. Set sync points on every click the viewer has to copy, and write short pauses into the script where the screen needs a moment, such as a page loading. Sync points are available on every Clueso plan, and editing the script or trimming a clip afterward keeps the audio aligned. ([Clueso pricing](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) , November 2026.)


## How do you stop an AI voice mispronouncing product names?


AI voices mispronounce product names, acronyms, and anything with unusual capitalization, and they do it confidently. A viewer who hears your product's name said wrong starts doubting the rest of the video.


Build a pronunciation dictionary once, at the start, and add every brand term before you produce at volume. Most tools accept a phonetic spelling, and some accept IPA for finer control. In Clueso, a word added to the[pronunciation dictionary](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) applies across all your projects, with IPA available for English and separate rules per language. The dictionary is included from the Solo plan up.


## How do you handle pauses, dead air, and clipped endings?


Slow screens leave the narration with nothing to say. A report takes eight seconds to generate, a file takes a while to save, and an AI voice doesn't fill silence on its own. Either trim the wait out of the recording, or write a line that covers it, such as what the report will show once it loads.


Endings get clipped more often than anything else, so listen to the final five seconds of every export.


## Do AI-narrated screen recordings still need captions?


Yes. Ship every video with synchronized captions and enough on-screen emphasis, such as zooms and callouts, that it works with the sound off. Generate the captions from the finished narration, not from the script you started with. The two drift apart during editing, and a caption file made from the original script ends up slightly out of step with what viewers hear.


Make captions something the viewer can turn on rather than burning them into the video. Research on multimedia learning finds that showing identical words as narration and on-screen text at once can reduce comprehension, an effect known as the redundancy principle ([Mayer, Heiser, and Lonn, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.1.187) ). Captions viewers can toggle meet the accessibility requirement without forcing that on everyone. Clueso generates[captions](https://www.clueso.io/features/video-captions) on every plan and exports them as SRT or VTT.


## Which voice should you use: a stock AI voice, a cloned voice, or your own?


Use one voice across the whole library, whichever you choose. This matters most when many people contribute. Picture a software rollout where 40 subject-matter experts each record a few of the videos. If each of them narrated their own, learners would move between 40 different rooms, microphones, and speaking paces from one lesson to the next.


A stock AI voice is the default, and it works for most internal training and product walkthroughs. A[cloned voice](https://www.clueso.io/features/voice-cloning) lets one consenting person, such as your head of training or a familiar presenter, narrate every video without recording each one; on Clueso it's part of the Enterprise plan. Your own voice still works on individual clips where a personal tone matters, and Clueso lets you keep your original audio on any clip while the rest uses the AI voice.


Customer-facing video deserves a separate decision. Teams are generally more comfortable with AI narration on internal training than on videos their customers see, where audio quality and trust carry more weight. We've written about[when AI voiceover belongs in customer-facing video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/should-we-use-ai-voiceover-in-customer-facing-videos) .


## How do you update the voiceover when the product changes?


This is where generated narration pays for itself. When narration was recorded by a person, updating one step means finding that person, matching their voice and their room, or re-recording the whole video, and most teams don't bother. When narration is generated from a script, you edit the line that changed and regenerate the audio for that clip only, and it sounds identical to the rest. For the visual side, see[updating a training video without re-recording it](https://www.clueso.io/blog/update-training-video-without-re-recording) .


Translation works the same way. Narration generated from a script can be regenerated in another language without booking a voice artist, and Clueso[translates the voiceover and captions into 150+ languages](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-translate) . Personio used this to cut a four-language video, in English, German, Spanish, and Dutch, from 5.5 days to within two days ([Personio's story](https://www.clueso.io/customers/personio) ). Keep a glossary so product names survive translation; see our guide to[translating a video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-translate-a-video) .


## Frequently asked questions


### Is there an AI tool that can create screen recording demos with AI voiceover?


Yes. Clueso records or imports a screen recording, transcribes your rough narration, rewrites it into a script, and reads it back with an AI voice synced to the screen. The alternative is a separate screen recorder plus a text-to-speech tool, with the syncing done by hand.


### How do I add AI voiceover and captions to a video in one tool?


Use a tool that generates both from the same script. In Clueso, the captions come from the finished narration, so they match what viewers hear, and you can export them as SRT or VTT files or translate them into 150+ languages.


### Does Clueso include AI voiceover on its base plan, or is it an add-on?


AI voiceovers are on every Clueso plan, including Free, which has 500+ voices; paid plans have 10,000+. The pronunciation dictionary starts on the Solo plan, and voice cloning is part of the Enterprise plan. ([Clueso pricing](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) , November 2026.)


### Which tool supports AI voiceover and translation together?


Clueso translates the voiceover, captions, and written guide of a video into 150+ languages from the same project, and on the Enterprise plan a translation glossary keeps product terms consistent. Check that any tool you evaluate regenerates the voice in the new language rather than only translating the captions.


Before you commit to a workflow, run one video through it end to end, including an update. Record a walkthrough, publish it, then change a single step and publish it again. Time the second part. That number tells you more about whether the workflow will hold up across a hundred videos than the first one does.
